title: ElementInternals ARIA semantics are opaque to DOM-based accessibility testing tools

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

labels.name: topic: custom elements
labels.description: Relates to custom elements (as defined in DOM and HTML)

body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

## Problem Statement
The Accessibility testing tools that run in the page context (e.g. axe-core and tools built on top of it) currently have no way to observe ARIA semantics applied via `ElementInternals`. This makes it impossible to accurately test custom elements that define their accessibility using ElementInternals, leading to false positives, false negatives, or outright exclusion of custom elements from automated accessibility scans.

Defining accessibility semantics via `ElementInternals` currently prevents existing testing tools from inspecting those semantics. As ElementInternals adoption grows in design systems and component libraries, automated accessibility testing for custom elements becomes increasingly unreliable. This only impacts `ElementInternals`, thus why we are reaching out to this group.

This topic has been raised and discussed multiple times in recent ARIA WG meetings. A summary of those discussions and relevant context can be found in w3c/aria#2663. Below is a brief summary of the shared understanding so far, and the kickoff of a discussion with the HTML WG on whether and how this problem could be addressed at the platform level.

## Summary from ARIA WG Discussions

Discussions in the ARIA Working Group have led to broad agreement on the following points:

- The problem is real and must be addressed; now that `ElementInternals` is baseline and sees more adoption it is worsening.
- Accessibility testing spans multiple layers, including testing assistive technologies, testing the computed accessibility tree, and testing author-provided semantics before accessibility tree computation. This issue is narrowly scoped to the last layer and does not seek access to the computed tree or AT-facing APIs.
- Solutions that rely on WebExtension- or WebDriver-specific APIs do not address the needs of widely reused page-context libraries. Many consumers cannot assume access to privileged inspection or debugging contexts.
- WebExtension- or WebDriver-specific approaches do not sufficiently address this problem. Widely adopted page-context libraries such as axe-core must remain backward-compatible across a large ecosystem of tools, many of which cannot assume access to privileged environments (e.g. DevTools, inspectors, or debugger permissions). Disrupting existing accessibility testing workflows at scale is undesirable, as accessibility testing is often introduced late in development and is particularly susceptible to being deprioritized or removed when integration becomes more complex.
- This creates a growing divergence between what authors can provide (and therefore what assistive technologies consume) and what automated testing tools can verify.
- Exposing the full accessibility tree or platform accessibility APIs to the web is not acceptable due to privacy and performance concerns.

While there is consensus that this is a legitimate problem that standard bodies should solve, the ARIA WG has not identified a clear path forward within ARIA itself, and the discussion has converged on whether this is more appropriately addressed at by the `ElementInternals` authors. 

## Proposal
A minimal way to address this would be to expose a read-only DOM API that reflects the ARIA attributes explicitly set via the `ElementInternals` ARIAMixin, enabling DOM-based accessibility testing of author-provided semantics. For example, consider this intentionally high-level API sketch:

```js
element.getElementInternalsAria()
```

This API could always return an object (regardless of whether ElementInternals was attached), with individual ARIA properties returning null when not set by the author. I think this solution preserves the encapsulation of `ElementInternals` as much as possible while solving its accessibility problems.

The goal of this issue is to kick off a constructive discussion toward a solution that addresses the core problem. Feedback and ideas from the WHATWG would be greatly appreciated.
